messages.content: Amory.
Yes, Beatrice.
Dear, don't think of getting out of bed yet. I've always suspected that early rising in early life makes one nervous. Clothilde is having your breakfast brought up.
All right.
Amory.
Oh, yes.
Indeed, Mrs. Blaine, he is still delightful company—quite the cardinal's right-hand man.
Amory will go to him one day, I know, and Monsignor Darcy will understand him as he understood me.
Aw—I b'lieve, doncherknow, the Umuricun revolution was lawgely an affair of the middul clawses.
Washington came of very good blood—aw, quite good—I b'lieve.
Oh, yeah, she's here.
But, she's the only one what is here. The party's gone.
What?
She's been waitin' for Amory Blaine. That's you, ain't it? Her mother says that if you showed up by five-thirty you two was to go after 'em in the Packard.
'Lo, Amory.
'Lo, Myra.
Well—you got here, anyways.
Well—I'll tell you. I guess you don't know about the auto accident.
Who was it to?
Well, uncle 'n aunt 'n I.
Your uncle?
Oh, no just a horse—a sorta gray horse.
Probably killed the engine.
We'll go now. You see, Amory, the bobs were ordered for five and everybody was here, so we couldn't wait—
Well, I couldn't help it, could I?
So mama said for me to wait till ha'past five. We'll catch the bobs before it gets to the Minnehaha Club, Amory.
What?
Nothing. I was just yawning. Are we going to surely catch up with 'em before they get there?
Myra. I beg a thousand pardons. Can you ever forgive me?
Why—yes—sure.
Oh, Amory, don't smoke. You'll stunt your growth!
I don't care. I gotta. I got the habit. I've done a lot of things that if my fambly knew I went to the burlesque show last week.
Oh, yes, you do! You got a crush on Froggy Parker. I guess everybody knows that.
No, I haven't.
Because I've got a crush, too—
Tell him to go to the Minnehaha straight. I wanta talk to you—I got to talk to you.

There's always a bunch of shy fellas, sitting at the tail of the bob, sorta lurkin' an' whisperin' an' pushin' each other off. Then there's always some crazy cross-eyed girl she's always talkin' hard, sorta, to the chaperon.
You're such a funny boy.
How d'y' mean?
Oh—always talking about crazy things. Why don't you come ski-ing with Marylyn and I to-morrow?
We're awful.
Kiss me again.
I don't want to.
I don't want to!
I hate you! Don't you ever dare to speak to me again!
What?
You are tall—but you're still very handsome—you've skipped the awkward age, or is that sixteen; perhaps it's fourteen or fifteen; I can never remember; but you've skipped it.
Don't embarrass me.
Amory, dear. I had such a strange, weird time after I left you.
Did you, Beatrice?
When I had my last breakdown
The doctors told me that if any man alive had done the consistent drinking that I have, he would have been physically shattered, my dear, and in his grave—long in his grave.
What, Amory?
I said go on, Beatrice.

That was all—it merely recurred and recurred—gardens that flaunted coloring against which this would be quite dull, moons that whirled and swayed, paler than winter moons, more golden than harvest moons—
Are you quite well now, Beatrice?
Poor Beatrice—poor Beatrice.
Tell me about you, Amory. Did you have two horrible years?
No, Beatrice. I enjoyed them. I adapted myself to the bourgeoisie. I became conventional.
Beatrice. I want to go away to school. Everybody in Minneapolis is going to go away to school.
But you're only fifteen.
Yes, but everybody goes away to school at fifteen, and I want to, Beatrice.
Amory, I have decided to let you have your way. If you still want to, you can go to school.
Yes?
When do I go to school?
Next month. You'll have to start East a little early to take your examinations. After that you'll have a free week, so I want you to go up the Hudson and pay a visit.
To who?
To Monsignor Darcy, Amory. He wants to see you. He went to Harrow and then to Yale—became a Catholic. I want him to talk to you—I feel he can be such a help— Dear Amory, dear Amory—
My dear boy, I've been waiting to see you for years. Take a big chair and we'll have a chat.
I've just come from school—St. Regis's, you know.
Hate 'em all. Like English and history.
Of course. You'll hate school for a while, too, but I'm glad you're going to St. Regis's.
Why?
Because it's a gentleman's school, and democracy won't hit you so early. You'll find plenty of that in college.
I'm one, you know.
Oh, you're different—I think of Princeton as being lazy and good-looking and aristocratic—you know, like a spring day. Harvard seems sort of indoors—
And Yale is November, crisp and energetic.
That's it.
I was for Bonnie Prince Charlie.
Of course you were—and for Hannibal—
You're not sorry to go, of course. With people like us our home is where we are not.
I am sorry—
No, you're not. No one person in the world is necessary to you or to me.
Well—
Amory. I've sent for you on a personal matter.
Yes, sir.
I've noticed you this year and I—I like you. I think you have in you the makings of a—a very good man.
Yes, sir.
But I've noticed, that you're not very popular with the boys.
No, sir.
I wonder about actresses; are they all pretty bad?
No, sir, not by a darn sight, and I know that girl's as good as gold. I can tell.
Got tobacco?
Sure.
I'm coming in.
Take a couple of pillows and lie in the window-seat, why don't you.
Hold up, Amory. That's too darned gloomy. How about yourself?
I'm in a superior class. You are, too. We're philosophers.
I'm not.
Sure you are. You've got a darn good head on you.
You're not a slicker.
A what?
A slicker.
What the devil's that?
Well, it's something that—that—there's a lot of them. You're not one, and neither am I, though I am more than you are.
Who is one? What makes you one?
Why—why, I suppose that the sign of it is when a fellow slicks his hair back with water.
Like Carstairs?
Chocolate sundae.
Double chocolate jiggah? Anything else?
Why—yes.
Bacon bun?
Got a hammer?
No—sorry. Maybe Mrs. Twelve, or whatever she goes by, has one.
My name's Holiday.
Blaine's my name.
Where'd you prep?
Andover—where did you?
St. Regis's.
Oh, did you? I had a cousin there.
Come along and have a bite with us.
All right.
I hear Commons is pretty bad.
That's the rumor. But you've got to eat there—or pay anyways.
Crime!
Imposition!
Lot of pep, though. I wouldn't have gone to Yale for a million.
Me either.
You going out for anything?
Not me—Burne here is going out for the Prince—the Daily Princetonian, you know.
Yes, I know.
You going out for anything?
Why—yes. I'm going to take a whack at freshman football.
Play at St. Regis's?
Some, but I'm getting so damned thin.
You're not thin.
Well, I used to be stocky last fall.
Oh!
Yoho!
Oh, honey-baby—you're so big and strong, but oh, so gentle!
Clinch!
Oh, Clinch!
Kiss her, kiss 'at lady, quick!
Oh-h-h—!
Want a sundae—I mean a jigger?
Sure.
Wonderful night.
It's a whiz.
You men going to unpack?
Guess so. Come on, Burne.
We're the damned middle class, that's what!
Well, why not? We came to Princeton so we could feel that way toward the small colleges—have it on 'em, more self-confidence, dress better, cut a swathe—
Oh, it isn't that I mind the glittering caste system. I like having a bunch of hot cats on top, but gosh, Kerry, I've got to be one of them.
But just now, Amory, you're only a sweaty bourgeois.
I won't be—long. But I hate to get anywhere by working for it. I'll show the marks, don't you know.
Honorable scars. There's Langueduc, if you want to see what he looks like—and Humbird just behind.
Oh. Humbird looks like a knock-out, but this Langueduc—he's the rugged type, isn't he? I distrust that sort. All diamonds look big in the rough.
Well, you're a literary genius. It's up to you.
I wonder if I could be. I honestly think so sometimes. That sounds like the devil, and I wouldn't say it to anybody except you.
Well—go ahead. Let your hair grow and write poems like this guy D'Invilliers in the Lit.
Read his latest effort?
Never miss 'em. They're rare.
Hello! he's a freshman, isn't he?
Yeah.
I can't drift—I want to be interested. I want to pull strings, even for somebody else, or be Princetonian chairman or Triangle president. I want to be admired, Kerry.
You're thinking too much about yourself.
What line do you throw 'em? I've tried everything, and the mad wags aren't even afraid of me.
You're the 'nice boy' type.
Are you referring to your bacon buns?
No. I was referring to Bernard Shaw.
I've never read any Shaw. I've always meant to. Did you ever read Stephen Phillips, or do you like poetry?
Yes, indeed. I've never read much of Phillips, though.
It's pretty fair, I think. Of course he's a Victorian. that awful highbrow, Thomas Parke D'Invilliers.
Ever read any Oscar Wilde?
No. Who wrote it?
It's a man—don't you know?
Oh, surely. Wasn't the comic opera, 'Patience,' written about him?
Yes, that's the fella. I've just finished a book of his, 'The Picture of Dorian Gray,' and I certainly wish you'd read it. You'd like it. You can borrow it if you want to.
Why, I'd like it a lot—thanks.
Don't you want to come up to the room? I've got a few other books.
Put on 'Hearts and Flowers'! Oh, my Lord, I'm going to cast a kitten.
Shut off the damn graphophone. I'm not giving an exhibition.
Oh, God!
I'm very damn wet!
HA-HA HORTENSE!
All right, ponies!
Shake it up!
Hey, ponies—how about easing up on that crap game and shaking a mean hip?
Why on earth are we here?
I don't know. I'm just full of the devil.
No—but is this your line for every girl? What have I done to deserve it?
And you didn't feel tired dancing or want a cigarette or any of the things you said? You just wanted to be—
Isabelle!
I'm ready.
I've heard a lot about you since you wore braids—
Wasn't it funny this afternoon—
How—from whom?
From everybody—for all the years since you've been away.
I'll tell you what I remembered about you all these years.
I've got an adjective that just fits you.
I don't know you very well yet.
Will you tell me—afterward?
Is Froggy a good friend of yours?
Rather—why?
Isabelle. I want to tell you something. that funny look in her eyes.
I don't know whether or not you know what you—what I'm going to say. Lordy, Isabelle—this sounds like a line, but it isn't.
I know.
Maybe we'll never meet again like this—I have darned hard luck sometimes.
You'll meet me again—silly.
I've fallen for a lot of people—girls—and I guess you have, too—boys, I mean, but, honestly, you— Oh, what's the use—you'll go your way and I suppose I'll go mine.
Isabelle. You know I'm mad about you. You do give a darn about me.
Yes.
How much do you care—do you like any one better?
No.
Isabelle, I'm going back to college for six long months, and why shouldn't we—if I could only just have one thing to remember you by—
Close the door....
Fourteen angels were watching o'er them.
Damn! Damn!
Hi, Dibby—'gratulations!
Goo' boy, Tom, you got a good bunch in Cap.
Say, Kerry—
Oh, Kerry—I hear you went Tiger with all the weight-lifters! Well, I didn't go Cottage—the parlor-snakes' delight.
They say Overton fainted when he got his Ivy bid—Did he sign up the first day?—oh, no. Tore over to Murray-Dodge on a bicycle—afraid it was a mistake.
How'd you get into Cap—you old roue?
'Gratulations!
'Gratulations yourself. Hear you got a good crowd.
Wake up, Original Sin, and scrape yourself together. Be in front of Renwick's in half an hour. Somebody's got a car.
Where'd you get the car?
Sacred trust, but don't be a critical goopher or you can't go!
I think I'll sleep.
Sleep!
Why not? I've got a class at eleven-thirty.
Who's going?
Oh, Dick Humbird and Kerry Holiday and Jesse Ferrenby and—oh about five or six. Speed it up, kid!

You see, the car belongs down there. In fact, it was stolen from Asbury Park by persons unknown, who deserted it in Princeton and left for the West. Heartless Humbird here got permission from the city council to deliver it.
Anybody got any money?
That makes it interesting.
Money—what's money? We can sell the car.
Charge him salvage or something.
How're we going to get food?
Honestly, do you doubt Kerry's ability for three short days? Some people have lived on nothing for years at a time. Read the Boy Scout Monthly.
Three days, and I've got classes.
One of the days is the Sabbath.
Just the same, I can only cut six more classes, with over a month and a half to go.
Throw him out!
It's a long walk back.
Amory, you're running it out, if I may coin a new phrase.
Hadn't you better get some dope on yourself, Amory?
No, I'm not. I'm thinking about the Princetonian. I ought to make up to-night; but I can telephone back, I suppose.
Oh, these important men—
Oh, good Lord! Look at it!
What?
Let me out, quick—I haven't seen it for eight years! Oh, gentlefolk, stop the car!
What an odd child!
Now we'll get lunch. Come on, Amory, tear yourself away and get practical.
We'll try the best hotel first, and thence and so forth.
Eight twenty-five.
Rotten overcharge. We'll give them two dollars and one for the waiter. Kerry, collect the small change.
No mistake!
Won't he send after us?
You see, Amory, we're Marxian Socialists. We don't believe in property and we're putting it to the great test.
Night will descend.
Oh, Alec, I believe I'm tired of college.
I think I am, too, in a way.
All I'd like would be a little home in the country, some warm country, and a wife, and just enough to do to keep from rotting.
Me, too.
I'd like to quit.
What does your girl say?
Oh! She wouldn't think of marrying... that is, not now. I mean the future, you know.
My girl would. I'm engaged.
Are you really?
Yes. Don't say a word to anybody, please, but I am. I may not come back next year.
But you're only twenty! Give up college?
Why, Amory, you were saying a minute ago—
Let's borrow bicycles and take a ride.
All right. I'm not a bit tired and this is almost the last night of the year, really, because the prom stuff starts Monday.
Oh, but you're missing the real point, Tom. You've just had your eyes opened to the snobbishness of the world in a rather abrupt manner. Princeton invariably gives the thoughtful man a social sense.
You consider you taught me that, don't you?
Didn't I?
Sometimes. I think you're my bad angel. I might have been a pretty fair poet.
Yes, you're right. I wouldn't have liked it. Still, it's hard to be made a cynic at twenty.
I was born one. I'm a cynical idealist.
It's good, this ride, isn't it?
Yes; it's a good finish, it's knock-out; everything's good to-night. Oh, for a hot, languorous summer and Isabelle!
You Princeton boys?
Yes.
Well, there's one of you killed here, and two others about dead.
My God!
It's Dick—Dick Humbird!
Oh, Christ!
I say, old man, I've got an awfully nice—
Sorry, Kaye, but I'm set for this one. I've got to cut in on a fella.
Well, the next one?
What—ah—er—I swear I've got to go cut in—look me up when she's got a dance free.
What's the matter?
Your shirt stud—it hurt me—look!
Oh, Amory, of course you couldn't help it, and it didn't hurt much; but what are we going to do about it?
Do about it? Oh—that spot; it'll disappear in a second.
It isn't, it's still there—and it looks like Old Nick—oh, Amory, what'll we do! It's just the height of your shoulder.
Massage it.
Isabelle, darling, I think it'll—
Don't touch me! Haven't I enough on my mind and you stand there and laugh!
Oh, shut up!
Damn!
I hate to be laughed at.
I won't laugh any more. I'm not laughing now, am I?
You did.
Oh, don't be so darned feminine.
I'm leaving early in the morning.
Why?
Why not?
There's no need.
However, I'm going.
Well, if you insist on being ridiculous—
Oh, don't put it that way.
—just because I won't let you kiss me. Do you think—
I really don't know what to think about you. You're so funny.
How?
Yes.
Well, you didn't seem to feel so self-confident to-night. Maybe you're just plain conceited.
No, I'm not. At Princeton—
Oh, you and Princeton! You'd think that was the world, the way you talk! Perhaps you can write better than anybody else on your old Princetonian; maybe the freshmen do think you're important—
You don't understand—
Yes, I do. I do, because you're always talking about yourself and I used to like it; now I don't.
Have I to-night?
That's just the point. You got all upset to-night. You just sat and watched my eyes. Besides, I have to think all the time I'm talking to you—you're so critical.
I make you think, do I?
You're a nervous strain and when you analyze every little emotion and instinct I just don't have 'em.
I know.
Let's go.
What train can I get?
There's one about 9:11 if you really must go.
Yes, I've got to go, really. Good night.
Good night.
Oh—ah—I'm damned if I know, Mr. Rooney.
Oh, why of course, of course you can't use that formula. That's what I wanted you to say.
Why, sure, of course.
Do you see why?
You bet—I suppose so.
If you don't see, tell me. I'm here to show you.
Well, Mr. Rooney, if you don't mind, I wish you'd go over that again.
Gladly. Now here's 'A'...
If you don't pass it, you're the world's worst goopher. Your stock will go down like an elevator at the club and on the campus.
Oh, hell, I know it. Why rub it in?
Oh, drop the subject. Watch and wait and shut up. I don't want every one at the club asking me about it, as if I were a prize potato being fattened for a vegetable show.
Oh, Tom, any mail?
What is it, blue or pink?
Don't know. Better come up.
'Lo, Kerry. Ah, men of Princeton. Registrar's Office.
We have here quite a slip of paper.
Open it, Amory.
Just to be dramatic, I'll let you know that if it's blue, my name is withdrawn from the editorial board of the Prince, and my short career is over.
Well?
Pink or blue?
Say what it is.
We're all ears, Amory.
Your own laziness.
No—something deeper than that. I've begun to feel that I was meant to lose this chance.
They're rather off you at the club, you know; every man that doesn't come through makes our crowd just so much weaker.
I hate that point of view.
Of course, with a little effort you could still stage a comeback.
No—I'm through—as far as ever being a power in college is concerned.
Not me. I'm mad at the concrete thing. My own idleness was quite in accord with my system, but the luck broke.
Your system broke, you mean.
Maybe.
Well, what are you going to do? Get a better one quick, or just bum around for two more years as a has-been?
I don't know yet...
Oh, Amory, buck up!
I've felt like leaving college, Monsignor.
Why?
All my career's gone up in smoke; you think it's petty and all that, but—
Not at all petty. I think it's most important. I want to hear the whole thing. Everything you've been doing since I saw you last.
You know you wouldn't like to go.
Sometimes I would—to-night I'd go in a second.
Well, you'd have to be very much more tired of life than I think you are. I know you.
I'm afraid you do. It just seemed an easy way out of everything—when I think of another useless, draggy year.
Yes, I know; but to tell you the truth, I'm not worried about you; you seem to me to be progressing perfectly naturally.
No. I've lost half my personality in a year.
Not a bit of it! You've lost a great amount of vanity and that's all.
Lordy! I feel, anyway, as if I'd gone through another fifth form at St. Regis's.
No. That was a misfortune; this has been a good thing. Whatever worth while comes to you, won't be through the channels you were searching last year.
What could be more unprofitable than my present lack of pep?
But, Monsignor, I can't do the next thing.

Amory, between you and me, I have only just learned to do it myself. I can do the one hundred things beyond the next thing, but I stub my toe on that, just as you stubbed your toe on mathematics this fall.
Why do we have to do the next thing? It never seems the sort of thing I should do.
We have to do it because we're not personalities, but personages.
Yes, that's it; when you feel that your garnered prestige and talents and all that are hung out, you need never bother about anybody; you can cope with them without difficulty.
But, on the other hand, if I haven't my possessions, I'm helpless!
Absolutely.
That's certainly an idea.
Why do I make lists? Lists of all sorts of things?
Because you're a mediaevalist. We both are. It's the passion for classifying and finding a type.
It's a desire to get something definite.
It's the nucleus of scholastic philosophy.
I was beginning to think I was growing eccentric till I came up here. It was a pose, I guess.
Don't worry about that; for you not posing may be the biggest pose of all. Pose—
Yes?
But do the next thing.
Table for four in the middle of the floor. Hurry, old dear, tell 'em we're here!
Tell 'em to play 'Admiration'! You two order; Phoebe and I are going to shake a wicked calf.
There's Findle Margotson, from New Haven! 'Lo, Findle! Whoo-ee!
Oh, Axia! C'mon over to our table. No!
There's a natural damn fool.
Oh, he's all right. Here's the old jitney waiter. If you ask me, I want a double Daiquiri.
Who's that pale fool watching us?
Where? We'll have him thrown out! Where is he?
Where now?
Up to the flat. We've got brandy and fizz—and everything's slow down here to-night.
Phoebe's great stuff.
I'm only going to stay half an hour.
Hell y' say. We're here now—don't le's rush.
I don't like this place, and I don't want any food.
Amory, pour 'em out, and we'll drink to Fred Sloane, who has a rare, distinguished edge.
Yes, and Amory. I like Amory.
Well, look at Amory! Poor old Amory's sick—old head going 'round?
Look at that man!
Thought you weren't drinking.
Come back! Come back! Amory, dear, you aren't going, Amory!
Come on, Amory, stick 'th us!
Sick, are you?
Sit down a second!
Take some water.
What do you mean?
This street, it's ghastly! Come on! let's get back to the Avenue!
Man! it's filthy, and if you can't see it, you're filthy, too!
I can't help it. What's the matter with you? Old remorse getting you? You'd be in a fine state if you'd gone through with our little party.
Had a hell of a dream about you last night. I had an idea you were in some trouble.
Don't tell me about it! Don't say a word; I'm tired and pepped out.
God help us!
Oh, my heavens! look behind! It's gone now. Something was looking at you.
Heard the latest?
No. Somebody flunked out? Or another ship sunk?
Worse than that. About one-third of the junior class are going to resign from their clubs.
What!
Actual fact!
Why!
Spirit of reform and all that. Burne Holiday is behind it. The club presidents are holding a meeting to-night to see if they can find a joint means of combating it.
Well, what's the idea of the thing?

Oh, clubs injurious to Princeton democracy; cost a lot; draw social lines, take time; the regular line you get sometimes from disappointed sophomores. Woodrow thought they should be abolished and all that.
But this is the real thing?
Absolutely. I think it'll go through.
For Pete's sake, tell me more about it.
And you say almost a third of the junior class are going to resign?
Call it a fourth and be safe.
You probably know what I want to talk to Tom about, and it isn't a bit private. I wish you'd stay.
I'd be glad to.
How about religion?
Don't know. I'm in a muddle about a lot of things—I've just discovered that I've a mind, and I'm starting to read.
Read what?
Everything. I have to pick and choose, of course, but mostly things to make me think. I'm reading the four gospels now, and the 'Varieties of Religious Experience.'
What chiefly started you?
Wells, I guess, and Tolstoi, and a man named Edward Carpenter. I've been reading for over a year now—on a few lines, on what I consider the essential lines.
Poetry?
Well, frankly, not what you call poetry, or for your reasons—you two write, of course, and look at things differently. Whitman is the man that attracts me.
Whitman?
Yes; he's a definite ethical force.
Are you coming to the Harvard game?
If you ask me.
Of course I do.
She'll see. This will be the last game she ever persuades any young innocent to take her to!
But, Burne—why did you invite her if you didn't want her?
Burne, you know you're secretly mad about her—that's the real trouble.
Don't you mind losing prestige?
Of course I don't. What's prestige, at best?
Of course health counts—a healthy man has twice the chance of being good.
I don't agree with you—I don't believe in 'muscular Christianity.'
I do—I believe Christ had great physical vigor.
Oh, no. He worked too hard for that. I imagine that when he died he was a broken-down man—and the great saints haven't been strong.
Well, let's waive it—we won't get anywhere, and besides I haven't quite made up my mind about it myself. Now, here's something I do know—personal appearance has a lot to do with it.
Coloring?
And the large mouth and broad chin and rather big nose undoubtedly make the superior face.
I'm not so sure.
Oh, yes—I'll show you.
Aren't they wonderful?
Burne, I think they're the ugliest-looking crowd I ever came across. They look like an old man's home.
Oh, Amory, look at that forehead on Emerson; look at Tolstoi's eyes.
I hate the dark. I didn't use to—except when I was particularly imaginative, but now, I really do—I'm a regular fool about it.
That's useless, you know.
Quite possibly.
We'll go east, and down that string of roads through the woods.
Any person with any imagination is bound to be afraid. And this very walking at night is one of the things I was afraid about. I'm going to tell you why I can walk anywhere now and not be afraid.
Go on.
Lordy. I couldn't have done that. I'd have come out half-way, and the first time an automobile passed and made the dark thicker when its lamps disappeared, I'd have come in.
Well, we're half-way through, let's turn back.
It's the whole thing. It's the one dividing line between good and evil. I've never met a man who led a rotten life and didn't have a weak will.
How about great criminals?
They're usually insane. If not, they're weak. There is no such thing as a strong, sane criminal.
Burne, I disagree with you altogether; how about the superman?
Well?
He's evil, I think, yet he's strong and sane.
I've never met him. I'll bet, though, that he's stupid or insane.
I've met him over and over and he's neither. That's why I think you're wrong.
I tell you, he's the first contemporary I've ever met whom I'll admit is my superior in mental capacity.
It's a bad time to admit it—people are beginning to think he's odd.
He certainly is getting in wrong.
Have you talked to him lately?
No.
Then you haven't any conception of him.
Whither bound, Tsar?
Over to the Prince office to see Ferrenby. He wrote this editorial.
Going to flay him alive?
